chunks: Ali ibn Ibrahim narrated from Muhammad ibn Isa, from Yunus, from Zur'ah, from Sama'ah, who said:

I asked Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) about the testimony of the people of the religion (of the witness). He said, and he said: 'It is not valid except for the people of their own religion. And if no others are found, their testimony is valid for the bequest (al-wasiyyah), because it is not fitting that the right of anyone should be lost.'

key_terms.أَهْل الْمِلَّة: People of the religion (referring to the religious community of the witness)
key_terms.ذَهَاب الْحَقّ: Loss or forfeiture of a right

ai.seo_question: When is the testimony of non-Muslims or people of a different religion valid in Shia Islamic jurisprudence?
ai.summary: This hadith from *Tahdhib al-Ahkam* clarifies the general principle that testimony is restricted to one's own religious community (*ahl al-millah*), a rule derived from the specific context of the verse on debt. However, it introduces a pragmatic exception for bequests (*al-wasiyyah*), where the testimony of one's own co-religion is accepted even in mixed contexts to prevent the loss of rights (*la yasluh dhahab haqq ahad*), reflecting the Shia juristic emphasis on preserving property rights when no other witnesses are available.
